claims.title: Shopper order data may be readable across the public storefront boundary
claims.description: `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses from the public internet to `process:storefront-api` and carries order contents, shipping addresses, and card last-four values. Its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If this flow is not protected in transit, an on-path attacker on the public-facing route can intercept shoppers' PII and financial order data without accessing their sessions. The captured order and address details can then be used to target affected shoppers and correlate later activity handled by `process:storefront-api`. This is conditional on verifying the transport protection state, not an assertion that encryption is absent.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high, conditional on the unknown transport setting, because `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses the public-internet boundary and a network observer needs no application credential. Impact is high because the flow carries PII and financial order data, including shipping addresses and card last-four values, for storefront customers.

mitigations.summary: Require modern TLS for shopper order submission
mitigations.detail: Verify and set `encryption_in_transit` for `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` to TLS 1.2 or later, with certificate validation at the shopper-facing endpoint.

mitigations.summary: Minimize payment-related fields in the request
mitigations.detail: Avoid carrying payment-related values unnecessarily in the order submission payload; use opaque payment references where the processor integration permits.

claims.title: Settlement callbacks may disclose payment-status data in transit
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from the public internet to `process:storefront-api`, carries financial settlement confirmations, and has unknown protocol and `encryption_in_transit`. If transport protection is absent or ineffective, a network observer can intercept settlement status and order-related payment information while it travels from `entity:card-processor` to the storefront. That information reveals payment timing and order state, enabling targeted fraud or social-engineering attempts against affected orders. This is conditional on the unverified transport attributes.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high, conditional on the unknown protocol and transport protection, because the callback crosses the public-internet boundary and interception needs no webhook credential. Impact is medium because the flow is tagged financial and exposes settlement information, but the stated payload is a confirmation rather than the full order corpus.

mitigations.summary: Require HTTPS with validated certificates for processor callbacks
mitigations.detail: Establish the callback protocol and require TLS 1.2 or later for `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook`; reject cleartext callback delivery.
Keep the callback payload to an opaque payment or order reference and settlement state, resolving additional details only through protected internal processing.

claims.title: Order submissions may be readable between the storefront and core service
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` into `boundary:core-services` and carries order contents, shopper identifiers, and shipping addresses. Its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If that attribute resolves to no effective transport encryption, an attacker with observation capability on the DMZ-to-core path can intercept customer PII and financial order data. The attacker can use the captured shopper and order identifiers to target records subsequently persisted through `process:order-service` into `store:orders-db`. This is conditional on the unknown encryption state; it does not assert cleartext gRPC traffic.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown transport state: the flow crosses from the DMZ to core services, but an attacker must first obtain a position able to observe that internal path. Impact is high because the flow carries shopper identifiers, shipping addresses, order contents, and financial data for submitted orders.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt and mutually authenticate the gRPC hop
mitigations.detail: Require TLS 1.2 or later with mTLS on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order`, so both confidentiality and the peer identity are verified across the zone boundary.

mitigations.summary: Use opaque order references where possible
mitigations.detail: Minimize raw shopper identifiers and address data in the service-to-service payload when `process:order-service` can resolve them through a protected server-side lookup.

claims.title: Order records may be readable on the order-service database connection
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` carries order rows, shipping addresses, and card last-four values to `store:orders-db`, while its protocol and `encryption_in_transit` are unknown. If the database connection is not encrypted, an attacker who gains an observation point on this internal connection can intercept the confidential PII and financial data exchanged during reads and writes. The captured records expose data held in `store:orders-db` and can enable targeted attacks on shoppers; this is conditional on verifying the connection's transport protection.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional on the unknown connection protection because the attacker needs an internal position able to observe the order-service-to-database path. Impact is high because `store:orders-db` is confidential and the flow carries shopper addresses and card last-four data alongside order rows.

mitigations.summary: Require TLS for the PostgreSQL connection
mitigations.detail: Configure and enforce encrypted database transport for `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`, with certificate validation by `process:order-service`.
Limit network paths to `store:orders-db` to the specific order-service identity and environment, reducing opportunities to observe the connection.

claims.title: A storage copy could expose all confidential orders if encryption at rest is absent
claims.description: `store:orders-db` is classified confidential, holds PII and financial data, and has `encryption_at_rest: unknown`. If the unknown resolves to storage without effective encryption, an attacker who obtains a database volume, backup, snapshot, or other operational copy can read orders, shopper addresses, and card last-four values without using the application's database login. The resulting corpus disclosure can support targeted fraud and compromise every shopper represented in the copied data. This claim is conditional on the unverified at-rest encryption state, not a claim that the database is currently unencrypted.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown `encryption_at_rest` value: obtaining an operational storage copy requires access to storage or backup handling, but does not require a live application credential if encryption is absent. Impact is high because `store:orders-db` is confidential and contains PII and financial order data for the store's shoppers.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce encryption at rest for orders data
mitigations.detail: Establish the actual `encryption_at_rest` posture for `store:orders-db` and require managed-key or customer-managed-key encryption for database storage.

mitigations.summary: Apply the same protection to operational copies
mitigations.detail: Require encryption and restricted export access for backups, snapshots, replicas, and decommissioned media associated with `store:orders-db`.

claims.title: The order-service database password can unlock the full orders corpus
claims.description: The application account used by `process:order-service` on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` has full read/write access to `store:orders-db`, and its password is kept in an environment variable on the worker. An attacker who recovers that static credential from the worker's environment can use it to read the database's order rows, shopper addresses, and card last-four data in bulk. The second-order reach is corpus-scale: one recovered credential reaches all data available to the shared application account rather than only a single shopper's order.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the application-account password is a standing credential kept in an environment variable on `process:order-service`, though the attacker must first recover that value. Impact is high because the application account has full read/write access to confidential `store:orders-db`, which holds PII and financial order data.

mitigations.summary: Replace the environment password with short-lived workload credentials
mitigations.detail: Use workload identity or short-lived database credentials issued from a dedicated secret-management system rather than retaining a static password in the worker environment.

mitigations.summary: Reduce the application account's database scope
mitigations.detail: Replace the full read/write grant with narrowly scoped roles, tables, columns, and operations required by `process:order-service`, so one recovered credential cannot read the entire corpus.
Audit and alert on bulk or atypical reads performed through the order-service database principal.
